rv.q: This is a production composed of small parts, one after another, each building into something bigger.
Few shows benefit from all these deprivations at once, and 'A Man of No Importance' does suffer slightly in its final third as it begins to reveal too much skeleton.

In the midst of the busy fall theater season, Classic Stage Company’s triumphant Off-Broadway revival of the underrated 2002 chamber musical “A Man of No Importance,” starring Jim Parsons and directed by John Doyle, comes as a most welcome and most unexpected surprise.
This revival — the first since its New York premiere in 2002 — has songs and performances that will rouse the soul, and that's of the utmost importance.

Its minor flaws notwithstanding, you will definitely want a ticket to enter the world of 'A Man of No Importance.' With any luck, as well, this world will expand to Broadway in the near future, so even more audience members can experience it!
Whatever the ups and downs of his work in years past, A Man of No Importance is a definite highlight in his tenure, and a great way to say goodbye.
To use the local argot, A Man of No Importance is a darlin' thing, and I hope Doyle's edit becomes the standard version.
As Alfie contemplates his sexuality, mounts an Oscar Wilde play, and seeks to better understand himself through art, the well-sung production glides along at a comfortable pace.
The musical also benefits from the direction of John Doyle, who stepped down as artistic director of Classic Stage in June, and leaves the company with this wonderful parting gift.
The progress made by this musical’s more subdued hero carries its own radiance, and overall, this intimate, lovely production does it justice.
A Man of No Importance is an example, at best a mildly pleasant, mildly moving pastime well below the standards Flaherty, Ahrens, and McNally set for themselves (with Drabinsky prodding?).
But Doyle’s production remains oddly lifeless — and even moments of violence pass by without so much as a blip to raise the blood pressure.

All his trademarks are there—onstage instruments, an intimate focus on characters, choreography consisting entirely of walking in circles and percussively slamming down wooden chairs—but lack intentionality, specificity, or potency.
His is an indolent, entitled performance.
In that space, the charm and energy of this show just can't be denied.
The show takes pleasure in expressing theater's power to create community and its ability to help its practitioners transcend the travails of daily life.
Still, the performances and score of A Man of No Importance lift it up, and Doyle’s production, his last as artistic director of Classic Stage Company, is on the whole a pleasure.
Revived by the Classic Stage Company and presented in its intimate space, the play takes on a warmth and closeness.
Those familiar with Doyle's theatrical style will recognize his familiar treatment, which often gets in the way of cluttered staging as the cast simultaneously juggles furniture and the score.
The reality is the disconnect exists and the production suffers as a result.

cn.t: Doyle's pared-down revival of this underrated chamber musical earns praise for its intimacy and Parsons' tender lead performance, though critics split on whether the stark minimalism enhances or diminishes the show's emotional impact.
